clues: At functional residual capacity, it normally equals +5 cmH2O
It is calculated as alveolar pressure minus intrapleural pressure
This distending pressure across the lung wall keeps alveoli open against elastic recoil
It increases in emphysema and decreases in pulmonary fibrosis and neonatal RDS
Its normal value for isolated human lungs is approximately 0.2 L/cmH2O
It measures lung distensibility as the change in lung volume per unit change in transpulmonary pressure
Inflating an excised lung with saline instead of air nearly abolishes this phenomenon
It occurs because higher pressure is needed to overcome surface tension during inflation than during deflation
It is the loop separation between the inspiratory and expiratory pressure-volume curves of the lung

terms.sub: Alveolar Surface Tension, Laplace's Law, and Surfactant
clues: For a spherical alveolus with one air-liquid interface, it states that P = 2T / r
It explains why small alveoli would empty into large alveoli if surface tension were constant
This physical law relates distending or collapsing pressure to wall surface tension and radius

terms.sub: Dynamic Airway Compression and Equal Pressure Point
clues: Pursed-lip breathing in emphysema shifts this point proximally toward cartilage-supported bronchi
Downstream of this site during forced expiration, non-cartilaginous airways undergo dynamic compression
It is the location along the airway where intraluminal pressure equals surrounding intrapleural pressure

terms.sub: Work of Breathing and Closing Capacity
clues: It equals closing volume plus residual volume
With aging or supine posture, it rises above functional residual capacity and causes dependent airway collapse during tidal breathing
It is the lung volume at which small airways at the lung base begin to close during expiration

terms.sub: Lung Volumes, Capacities, and Dead Space
clues: It equals expiratory reserve volume plus residual volume (~2,300 mL) and cannot be measured by simple spirometry
At this volume, inward lung elastic recoil exactly balances outward chest wall recoil
It is the volume of air remaining in the lungs at the end of a normal passive expiration

terms.sub: Lung Volumes, Capacities, and Dead Space
clues: It is calculated clinically using the Bohr equation from arterial and mixed-expired PCO2
In healthy individuals it nearly equals anatomical dead space (~150 mL), but it increases markedly in pulmonary embolism
It represents the total volume of ventilated air in each breath that does not participate in gas exchange
